hypothesis: For graphs that are discretisations of ordinary d-dimensional space (hypercubic lattices Z^d) the number of nodes within graph distance r grows like r^d, while for tree-like and randomly connected graphs the growth is exponential, so no finite exponent d exists; the biconditional ('precisely') additionally requires that polynomial growth of degree d occur only for networks corresponding to ordinary d-dimensional space.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. Primary (necessity and the tree/random clause): for the hypercubic lattices Z^1, Z^2, Z^3, Z^4 the growth exponent, estimated as the ordinary-least-squares slope of log N(r) against log r over r in [R/2, R] (R = 32 for d <= 3, R = 20 for d = 4), lies within 0.15 of d; for the infinite 3-regular tree (R = 13) and for a random 4-regular graph on n = 300000 nodes (R = largest radius with N(R) <= n/10) the same slope estimated over r in [R/2, R] exceeds 5, and log N(r) is better fit (higher R^2) by a straight line in r than in log r. If every one of these six conditions holds the primary test passes. Secondary (sufficiency / 'precisely'): the Cayley graph of the discrete Heisenberg group with generators x, y and inverses is known not to be quasi-isometric to any Z^d (Pansu 1983), yet has polynomial growth of degree 4 (Bass 1972 / Guivarc'h 1973). If its measured slope over r in [12, 24] lies in [3.5, 4.5], then a network with r^d growth exists that does not correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space in the strict sense. Verdict rule: primary passes and secondary slope in [3.5, 4.5] -> 'mixed' (the necessity direction and the tree/random clause hold; the sufficiency direction holds only if 'corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space' is read as 'has growth dimension d'); primary passes and secondary slope outside [3.5, 4.5] -> 'supports'.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any lattice exponent differs from d by more than 0.5, or if either the tree or the random 4-regular graph has a slope below 3 over the stated range (i.e. appears to have a small finite dimension), or if log N(r) for the tree or random graph is better fit by a straight line in log r than in r. Any other outcome (e.g. a lattice exponent off by between 0.15 and 0.5) -> 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
interpretation: Wolfram's 'number of nodes that appear out to distance r' is the size N(r) of the closed ball of graph-distance radius r around a node. 'Grows in some limiting sense like r^d' is operationalised as the local log-log slope of N(r) at the largest radii computed, which for an exact polynomial of degree d tends to d from below. 'Corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space' is taken, for the primary test, as 'is the nearest-neighbour graph of Z^d'; for the secondary test we use the standard geometric-group-theory meaning (quasi-isometric to R^d) and rely on published theorems for the Heisenberg group's status. 'Tree-like or randomly connected' is operationalised as the infinite 3-regular tree (BFS-generated) and a configuration-model random 4-regular graph. All graphs are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

datasets.name: Graph families generated by analysis.py: hypercubic lattices Z^1..Z^4 (nearest-neighbour, L1 adjacency), infinite 3-regular tree, random 4-regular configuration-model graph (n = 300000, numpy seed 20261031), discrete Heisenberg group Cayley graph (generators x, y and inverses)
datasets.role: ball sizes N(r) measured by breadth-first search from the origin node; radii up to R = 32 (Z^1..Z^3), 20 (Z^4), 24 (Heisenberg), and until N(r) > n/10 for the tree and random graph
